text: serendipity (noun): the faculty of making fortunate discoveries by accident. Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 after the Persian fairy tale The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes were always making discoveries by accident. Serendip is an old name for Sri Lanka, from Arabic Sarandib.
ephemeral (adjective): lasting for a very short time. From Greek ephemeros, meaning lasting only a day, from epi (on) and hemera (day).
lexicography (noun): the practice of compiling dictionaries. From Greek lexikon (of words) and graphia (writing), from graphein, to write.
etymology (noun): the study of the origin of words and how their meanings changed over time. From Greek etymon, the true sense of a word, and logia, the study of.
lexicon (noun): the vocabulary of a language, person or branch of knowledge; a dictionary. From Greek lexikon, neuter of lexikos, of words, from lexis, word or speech.
ubiquitous (adjective): present, appearing or found everywhere. From Latin ubique, everywhere, from ubi (where).
eloquent (adjective): fluent and persuasive in speaking or writing. From Latin eloquens, from eloqui, to speak out, from e (out) and loqui (to speak).
pharmacy (noun): a place where medicines are prepared and sold. From Greek pharmakeia, the use of drugs, from pharmakon, drug or medicine.
